claims.text: The catalytic performance of transition-metal catalysts is governed by the alignment of the metal d-band center relative to the Fermi level.
The d-band-center position modulates the binding strength of reactants and intermediates.
Systematically shifting the d-band center alters adsorption energies.
Changes in adsorption energy caused by d-band shifts affect catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability.
A standardized deposition method can produce transition-metal nanoparticles with uniform size and dispersion.
Introducing a small amount of a secondary metal can raise or lower the catalyst's d-band center.
Holding particle size and morphology constant would isolate electronic-structure changes as the principal difference between alloyed samples.
The surface d-band-center position governs the adsorption energies of reactants and intermediates.
A d-band-center shift changes the overlap between metal d orbitals and adsorbate molecular orbitals.
Changed metal-adsorbate orbital overlap modifies adsorption energy.
Modified adsorption energy affects rate-limiting catalytic steps.
Adsorption that is too weak causes insufficient reactant activation.
Adsorption that is too strong blocks active sites.
Either excessively weak or excessively strong adsorption compromises catalytic performance.
Catalysts shifted away from the proposed optimal d-band-center energy will have lower activity, altered selectivity, or reduced durability relative to the baseline.
Balanced adsorption permits both reactant activation and facile intermediate release.
The proposed relationship should hold when surface adsorption energies dominate reaction kinetics.
The proposed relationship may not apply under mass-transfer limitations or when significant morphological changes occur.
Surface segregation, support effects, and temperature-induced reconstruction can influence the quantitative relationship between d-band shifts and catalytic performance.
XPS or UPS can be used to quantify d-band-center positions in the proposed catalyst series.
